Replies to letter of November 18, 1974, Slator Blackiston, Jr. (State Dept.) to T. O. Jones (NSF)
It is obviously better to avoid the problem of dealing with an oil slick than it would be to control it after it appeared. Therefore, precautions will be taken to monitor the sediment cores as they are brought up so that gas analyses can be made with a chromatograph. We have been advised by a geochemist to "... analyze the gases from the muds for hydrocarbons methane through hexane. If appreciable amounts of hydrocarbons heavier than methane are present, say 10% or more of the total hydrocarbons, it suggests that the gas is seeping from a deeper accumulation. Consequently, if you have continuous gas shows, and these gases contain the ethane plus hydrocarbons, I would shift to another drill site before going on too deep."
The same source of the above information mentioned that methane might be encountered nearly continuously in the near surface, "but if it is encountered all the way down the hole, I would abandon the site before going much beyond 300 ft."
If substantial hydrocarbons are encountered, or released, the hole would be plugged and abandoned, as mentioned on p. 31 of the Draft Environmental Statement.
If hydrocarbons are released, they will be confined to the immediate area of the drill hole on the surface, and at the ice-water interface beneath the ice shelf. In either case, little immediate damage to the environment is foreseen. In the first case, as stated on p. 30 of the Draft, liquid hydrocarbons would spread out and percolate into the firm where it would be essentially trapped in the ice shelf until it reached the open sea, perhaps 1000 years later. Its effects at that time cannot be predicted. In the latter case, there may be no effects of hydrocarbons under the shelf ice if life does not exist there. Effects on life, if it does exist, would be unfortunate, but most likely of limited scope.
